articles.title: Resume Skills That Get Interviews: Before and After Rewrites
articles.excerpt: Most resumes are never read; they are scanned for a few seconds while the reviewer decides whether to keep going. That decision rests on what jumps out of the first screen: job titles, companies, date…
articles.body: Most resumes are never read; they are scanned for a few seconds while the reviewer decides whether to keep going. That decision rests on what jumps out of the first screen: job titles, companies, dates, and anything with a number in it. The candidates collecting interviews are rarely the most qualified people in the pile. They are the ones whose resumes read like evidence instead of essays. The gap between an ignored resume and a called-back one is usually a small set of fixable habits, not a missing degree. This guide covers the changes with the biggest payoffs: replacing adjectives with evidence, matching the job posting's language, putting numbers on ordinary work, and rewriting bullets. Each technique comes with a before-and-after example, plus a section for career changers.
articles.author: G105g

articles.title: How to Negotiate Your First Salary Offer (Without Blowing It)
articles.excerpt: Your first real salary offer is the single highest-leverage conversation of your early career. One good negotiation can be worth more than a year of raises, because every future raise and bonus is cal…
articles.body: Your first real salary offer is the single highest-leverage conversation of your early career. One good negotiation can be worth more than a year of raises, because every future raise and bonus is calculated as a percentage of your starting number. Yet most first-job candidates either accept instantly or fumble through a negotiation so awkward they wish they had not tried. The fix is not charisma. It is preparation plus a few short scripts you rehearse out loud before the call: what to do before the offer, what to say in the first thirty seconds, how to counter, and how to close without damaging the relationship. Why the first number matters so much Companies usually budget raises as a percentage of current salary - commonly 3 to 5 percent a year.

articles.title: How to Safely Store or Share a .env File (Without Slack or Email Leaks)
articles.excerpt: The .env file contains all the credentials used across your application. It can prove fatal if received by any unauthorised entity. So, don’t share the credentials, or share them safely. To avoid unau…
articles.body: The .env file contains all the credentials used across your application. It can prove fatal if received by any unauthorised entity. So, don’t share the credentials, or share them safely. Why .env and why should it be kept secure? To avoid unauthorised access to your services Keeping your code and credentials separate To easily change the configuration and credentials Best practices for the purpose: Do not share; just use different credentials for different individuals Share through a secure platform Share by encrypting the credentials Developers frequently paste .env snippets into Slack, Microsoft Teams, or email threads. Once pasted: It remains permanently stored in chat logs It gets indexed by third-parties. It is exposed if any chat bot or integration is compromised.

articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend What I Built FriendFocus is a small AI-powered study planner I built for a friend who often feels overwhelmed when there is too much to study and too little time. Instead of giving a generic timetable, FriendFocus takes a student's situation in natural language, such as: “I have an exam tomorrow, 3 chapters to cover, and only 2 hours.” It then uses Gemma 4 26B A4B IT to create a realistic, time-based study plan with focused study blocks, breaks, revision, and simple anti-procrastination advice. I wanted to build something practical and small enough that a student could actually use it when they are stressed about an upcoming exam.

articles.title: How I Rediscovered Kepler's Third Law on a Phone, in 204 Lines
articles.excerpt: How I Rediscovered Kepler's Third Law on a Phone, in 204 Lines A minimal symbolic regression engine that runs on Termux, with no GPU and no cloud. Most ML models are black boxes. You feed them data, t…
articles.body: How I Rediscovered Kepler's Third Law on a Phone, in 204 Lines A minimal symbolic regression engine that runs on Termux, with no GPU and no cloud. The problem with machine learning today Most ML models are black boxes. You feed them data, they give you predictions, but they never tell you why. For some tasks, that's fine. For others — physics, biology, finance — it's a problem. You don't want a prediction. You want a law. That's what symbolic regression does. It doesn't fit parameters. It finds the equation itself. It's a well-established field. Tools exist: PySR (Julia backend, state of the art) gplearn (Python, sklearn-compatible) FastSymbolicGP (2026, mobile preset) Eureqa (historical, closed source) But they all share a common trait: they need a real computer. A GPU helps.

articles.excerpt: On Febraury 13, 2000, the final Peanuts comic strip ran in newspapers, concluding 50 years of the lovable characters.
articles.body: While that was the first official Peanuts comic, a similar comic by Charles Schulz predated Peanuts and ran in Minnesota’s St. Paul Pioneer Press. It was called Li’l Folks and it also starred cute little children, although it did not have a regular cast like Peanuts would. Li’l Folks ran from 1947 until 1950, when Schulz quit after his editor refused to give him a raise from the $10 per comic he was making. After that, Schulz brought Li’l Folks to United Feature Syndicate. The national cartoon syndicator liked the comic, but needed to change its name because of a 1930s comic strip called Little Folks .

I had high hopes — and expectations — for the phone even before its launch, primarily because I have long wanted to use small phones that don’t feel sub-premium. What I didn’t expect was how hard it would hit me to switch back to a “regular” phone. Every moment I have spent with the Fold 8 has changed my perception of what a phone should feel like in the hand. It's understandable if you're feeling a bit cynical about everyone suddenly coming out of the woodwork to warn about how dangerous the thing they helped build is. They did, after all, make this mess. But that doesn't mean we should discount their warnings. Robinson says that the culture in industry is fundamentally broken. articles.body: 5 Min Read Heading Home: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 Concludes Station Science Mission NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission is ending, with the crew scheduled to return in early October. NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev will head home from the International Space Station after supporting research that benefits life on Earth and prepares humans for missions into deep space. articles.title: NASA’s DAVINCI Probe Can Stand the Heat
articles.excerpt: The engineering development unit for NASA’s DAVINCI (Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging) probe is photographed prior to a major thermal evaluation. The DAVINCI…
articles.body: An engineering model of NASA’s DAVINCI (Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging) descent probe passed a key test that ran from Aug. 28 to Sept. 10, showing it can survive the extreme temperatures of Venus. NASA/Mike Guinto The engineering development unit for NASA’s DAVINCI (Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging) probe is photographed prior to a major thermal evaluation. The DAVINCI team put the yoga ball-sized vessel into a ceramic-lined chamber with heat-scorched walls and ratcheted up the temperature to 869 F, or 465 C, over the course of about an hour — the same pace the probe will heat up during its descent to the surface of Venus.
